qs.q: An elderly patient with acute influenza A presents in respiratory distress. During viral entry into respiratory cells, which viral surface glycoprotein mediates initial attachment?
o: Hemagglutinin binding to cell surface sialic acid-containing glycoproteins
Neuraminidase cleaving terminal sialic acid residues on mucus
Matrix protein 2 forming proton channels to acidify the viral core
Nucleoprotein encapsidating negative-sense viral RNA segments
Lipid envelope fusing directly with the host plasma membrane surface
qs.e: Influenza hemagglutinin mediates initial viral attachment by binding to sialic acid residues on the surface of respiratory epithelial cells.

qs.q: Public health agencies monitor influenza strains for pandemic potential. Antigenic shift, resulting in major novel subtypes, is most likely driven by:
o: Point mutations accumulating within viral hemagglutinin receptor sites
Host immune pressure selecting for minor amino acid drift variants
Reassortment of segmented viral genomes during coinfection of a single cell
Spontaneous deletion of non-structural protein genes during passage
Recombination between influenza RNA and host messenger transcripts
qs.e: Antigenic shift occurs when segmented genomes of different influenza strains reassort during coinfection, creating novel pandemic subtypes.

qs.q: A child develops progressive neurological symptoms weeks after recovering from acute influenza infection. What is the underlying immunopathological mechanism?
o: Direct viral lysis of cerebral neurons
Ischemic infarction from endothelial damage
Bacterial superinfection causing meningitis
Autoimmune demyelination via molecular mimicry
Granulomatous inflammation destroying cortex
qs.e: Post-influenza encephalopathy often involves immune-mediated demyelination or cytokine storms rather than direct neural infection.

qs.q: A 4-year-old child presents with acute encephalopathy following a mild influenza infection, leading to rapid cerebral edema. What underlying pathophysiology is most characteristic of this condition?
o: Direct viral invasion of the frontal cortex occurs via the cribriform plate
Rapid mitochondrial dysfunction results in widespread cytotoxic cerebral edema
Immune-mediated demyelination affects central white matter fiber tracts
Thrombotic occlusion of major dural venous sinuses occurs due to immune complexes
Severe systemic hypotension leads to watershed cerebral tissue infarction
qs.e: Influenza-associated encephalopathy involves metabolic and mitochondrial failure leading to severe cellular swelling rather than direct infection.

qs.q: A public health laboratory is typing influenza isolates during an annual epidemic. Which viral surface glycoprotein is responsible for binding to host cell sialic acid receptors and mediating viral entry?
o: Neuraminidase removes sialic acid groups to facilitate release of progeny virions from infected cells.
Hemagglutinin attaches to terminal sialic acid residues on host cell surface glycoproteins for entry.
Matrix protein 2 creates proton channels that lower the interior pH of the viral particle.
Nucleoprotein packages the segmented negative‑sense RNA genome within the viral core.
Non‑structural protein 1 suppresses host interferon production during the early phase of infection.
qs.e: Influenza hemagglutinin (HA) mediates viral attachment and entry by binding to sialic acid receptors on the host cell surface.

qs.q: A patient with suspected influenza is treated with oseltamivir. The drug inhibits a specific viral enzyme. What is the primary consequence of this inhibition on the viral life cycle?
o: Prevent viral particle release from host cells
Inhibit viral protein synthesis on ribosomes
Block viral RNA replication in the cytoplasm
Disrupt viral envelope fusion with host membrane
Interfere with viral capsid assembly in nucleus
qs.e: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, preventing the release of new viral particles from the surface of infected host cells.

qs.q: A public health surveillance team monitors a novel influenza strain that has emerged in Southeast Asia, causing widespread pandemic disease through major genomic segment exchange. Which virological phenomenon describes this genetic alteration?
o: Recombination via template switching during negative-strand synthesis
Antigenic drift driven by point mutations in viral polymerase enzymes
Phenotypic mixing resulting from simultaneous coinfection of a single cell
Complementation occurring between defective viral particles in vivo
Antigenic shift involving the reassortment of segmented RNA genomes
qs.e: Antigenic shift occurs via segment reassortment, typically in coinfected animal hosts, creating novel pandemic strains.

qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents with acute influenza pneumonia. During viral entry into respiratory epithelial cells, which structural components mediate initial attachment to host sialic acid receptors?
o: Surface glycoproteins embedded in the lipid bilayer
Matrix protein 1 lining the inner viral envelope
Polymerase acidic proteins bound to viral segments
Nucleoprotein complexes protecting the viral RNA
qs.e: Hemagglutinin and neuraminidase are surface glycoproteins that facilitate viral attachment and release. Matrix and nucleoproteins are internal structural elements not involved in receptor binding.

ai.title: Influenza
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Influenza is an acute viral respiratory illness caused by orthomyxoviruses. In low‑resource settings it mimics malaria, pneumonia and bacterial sepsis; rapid clinical assessment and supportive care are key.

sections.p: Influenza is a self‑limited infection of the upper and lower respiratory tract caused by influenza A or B viruses. In East Africa it often presents with fever, myalgia, cough and can be complicated by bacterial pneumonia, especially in malnourished or HIV‑positive patients.
b: Seasonal peaks in rainy months
High attack rate in children and young adults

sections.p: Orthomyxoviruses are enveloped, segmented, negative‑sense RNA viruses with haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) surface proteins. Antigenic drift leads to yearly vaccine updates.
b: Segmented genome allows reassortment
HA/NA subtypes (H1N1, H3N2) determine virulence

sections.p: Spread by respiratory droplets and fomites. Virus enters ciliated epithelium, replicates, and is shed for 5–7 days. In low‑resource settings, crowded housing and lack of hand hygiene increase spread.
b: Droplet > 5 µm
Fomite persistence up to 48 h

sections.p: Typical influenza causes fever, myalgia, sore throat, dry cough and malaise. Severe disease includes viral pneumonia, ARDS and secondary bacterial pneumonia. In HIV or malnutrition, mortality rises.
b: Influenza‑associated pneumonia 10–20% of severe cases
Bacterial superinfection mainly S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, Klebsiella

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis is based on sudden onset of fever, myalgia and cough. In low‑resource settings rapid antigen tests are often unavailable; a simple clinical score can guide treatment.
b: Influenza‑like illness (ILI) definition: fever >38 °C + cough or sore throat, onset <7 days

t.b: A positive result supports antiviral therapy; a negative result still warrants treatment if clinical suspicion is high
Positive confirms strain and guides public health response

sections.p: Supportive care is mainstay. Antivirals (oseltamivir) are recommended within 48 h of symptom onset, especially in high‑risk groups. Vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention.
b: Avoid NSAIDs in severe cases due to bleeding risk

sections.p: On exam, look for rapid onset, high fever, myalgia, dry cough and conjunctivitis. In low‑resource settings, a simple ILI score plus history of recent contact can guide empiric therapy. Remember that bacterial pneumonia may present with productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia.
b: Do not delay antiviral therapy beyond 48 h in high‑risk patients

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxia (SpO₂ <90%), respiratory distress, confusion, persistent vomiting, haemoptysis, shock

faq.a: Rarely, influenza can cause transient hepatitis, but it is not a common complication.
Yes, it is considered safe; benefits outweigh risks in severe influenza.

faq.q: Do I need a chest X‑ray for all influenza patients?
faq.a: Only if there are signs of pneumonia, hypoxia or severe disease; otherwise, clinical assessment suffices.

exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman presents with fever, cough and chest pain. What is the next best step? — Start empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) and consider oseltamivir if within 48 h; obtain chest X‑ray if hypoxia or pleuritic pain.

A patient with influenza develops sudden haemoptysis. What is the most likely diagnosis and management? — Post‑influenza bacterial pneumonia (often S. aureus); start IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone, monitor airway.

A child with influenza has persistent fever after 5 days. What is the most appropriate investigation? — Rapid antigen test if available; otherwise, consider bacterial superinfection and start empiric antibiotics.
An elderly patient with influenza has SpO₂ 88% on room air. What is the immediate management? — Oxygen therapy to >94%, consider ICU transfer if no improvement.
A 35‑year‑old man with influenza is allergic to penicillin. What antibiotic should you use for suspected bacterial pneumonia? — Azithromycin alone or doxycycline if atypical organisms are suspected.
A patient with influenza is on chronic NSAIDs. What is the concern? — NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and may mask fever; consider acetaminophen instead.
A pregnant woman with influenza is concerned about antiviral safety. What do you advise? — Oseltamivir is safe in pregnancy; benefits outweigh risks.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam allow rapid differentiation of uncomplicated influenza from severe or secondary disease in low‑resource settings.
b: Onset: sudden vs gradual; note exact time of fever, myalgia and cough onset.
Maximum temperature recorded; >38 °C supports ILI definition.
Presence of chest pain, dyspnoea or haemoptysis suggests pneumonia or haemorrhage.
Risk factors: HIV, pregnancy, chronic lung disease, diabetes, malnutrition, recent NSAID or steroid use.
Vaccination status and recent antiviral use.
Exposure history: household contacts, school, market, recent travel during rainy season.
Medication history: oseltamivir timing, aspirin/NSAID use, herbal remedies.

t.b: Look for respiratory distress, cyanosis, altered mental status; positive if tachypnoea >30/min, use of accessory muscles, or inability to speak full sentences.
Confirms fever; >38 °C supports influenza, but normal temperature does not exclude severe disease.
Identify crackles, bronchial breath sounds or wheeze; crackles suggest viral or bacterial pneumonia, wheeze may indicate bronchospasm.
Detect dullness indicating consolidation; cannot differentiate viral from bacterial aetiology.
Answers oxygenation status; SpO₂ ≥93 % (≥95 % in pregnancy) is target; values below indicate need for supplemental O₂.
Answers presence of influenza virus; positive supports diagnosis, negative does not rule out infection in low‑resource settings.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise approach: bedside tests first, then laboratory or imaging if available; always interpret results in clinical context and local resource limits.
b: Complete blood count – leukopenia or relative lymphopenia favours viral aetiology; neutrophilia suggests bacterial superinfection.
Chest X‑ray – infiltrates in one or more lobes indicate pneumonia; bilateral diffuse opacities may be viral ARDS.
Nasopharyngeal swab for RT‑PCR – gold standard; detects influenza A/B and sub‑type, guides antiviral choice.
Serum electrolytes and renal function – required before oseltamivir in severe renal impairment.
Blood cultures – indicated when fever persists >48 h or sepsis suspected; positive culture confirms bacterial superinfection.

t.b: Answers whether infection is likely viral (lymphopenia) or bacterial (neutrophilia); if unavailable, rely on clinical signs of sepsis.
Answers presence and pattern of pneumonia; consolidation = bacterial or severe viral; diffuse interstitial pattern = viral; if unavailable, treat as severe influenza with oxygen.
Answers definitive viral identification and subtype; positive confirms diagnosis; if unavailable, treat empirically based on ILI criteria.
Answers oxygenation; SpO₂ <93 % (or <95 % in pregnancy) triggers supplemental O₂ and possible ICU transfer; if unavailable, assess respiratory rate and cyanosis.

sections.p: Severity classification guides antiviral timing, need for oxygen, and referral; use WHO/CDC criteria adapted for low‑resource settings.
b: Uncomplicated influenza: ILI criteria met, SpO₂ ≥93 %, respiratory rate ≤30/min, no chest infiltrates, no high‑risk comorbidity.
Severe influenza: SpO₂ <93 % (or <95 % in pregnancy), respiratory rate >30/min, mental status change, or hemodynamic instability.
Critical influenza: ARDS (PaO₂/FiO₂ <300), septic shock, or multi‑organ failure requiring ICU care.
High‑risk groups: age <5 yr, >65 yr, pregnancy, HIV CD4 <200, chronic heart/lung disease, diabetes, malnutrition.

sections.p: Several acute respiratory illnesses mimic influenza; systematic comparison of key features helps avoid misdiagnosis.
b: COVID‑19 – similar fever and cough but often loss of taste/smell, longer incubation, and may have ground‑glass opacities on imaging.
Rickettsial disease – fever with headache, rash, eschar; history of tick bite; responds to doxycycline, not antivirals.
Bacterial pneumonia – abrupt fever, productive sputum, lobar consolidation on X‑ray; neutrophilia and high CRP.
Pulmonary TB – sub‑acute fever, night sweats, weight loss, upper‑lobe infiltrates; sputum AFB positive.

t.b: Answers presence of SARS‑CoV‑2; positive excludes influenza as sole cause; if unavailable, consider epidemiology and loss of smell.
Answers rickettsial infection; positive with eschar and rash; if unavailable, treat empirically with doxycycline when suspicion high.
Answers bacterial pathogen; predominant Gram‑positive cocci in chains suggests pneumococcus; if unavailable, start empiric antibiotics if severe.
Answers radiologic differentiation; lobar consolidation favours bacterial, diffuse interstitial favours viral; if unavailable, base severity on clinical criteria.

sections.p: A systematic approach ensures rapid stabilisation, appropriate antiviral therapy, and timely escalation for severe influenza in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Immediate assessment: airway, breathing, circulation; give supplemental oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥93% (≥95% in pregnancy).
2. Obtain focused history (symptom onset, risk factors, vaccination, pregnancy, HIV, TB, drug use).
3. Perform rapid bedside exam: temperature, respiratory rate, pulse, auscultation for crackles, assess for signs of dehydration or shock.
4. Start oseltamivir as soon as possible, ideally within 48 h, for all high‑risk patients and any severe case.
5. Provide supportive care – antipyretics (paracetamol), adequate hydration, monitor fluid balance.

6. If hypoxia, respiratory distress, or worsening radiograph, consider empiric antibiotics covering typical bacterial superinfection (e.g., S. pneumoniae, S. aureus). Avoid macrolides if local resistance high.
7. Monitor vitals q4‑6 h, urine output, mental status; repeat chest imaging if deterioration.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognising adverse effects of antivirals and supportive drugs allows prompt mitigation and continuation of therapy.
b: Oseltamivir – nausea, vomiting, rare neuropsychiatric events; give with food, monitor mental status, switch to inhaled zanamivir if intolerable.
Paracetamol – hepatic toxicity at high cumulative doses; check baseline liver enzymes in chronic liver disease, limit total daily dose.
NSAIDs – increase risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and renal impairment; avoid in severe influenza, especially with thrombocytopenia or renal dysfunction.
Empiric β‑lactam antibiotics – allergic reactions; if penicillin allergy, use a respiratory fluoroquinolone (if not contraindicated) or vancomycin for MRSA risk.
Corticosteroids – may blunt inflammation but increase viral replication and secondary infection; reserve for refractory septic shock only.

sections.p: Complications often herald the need for intensive support or referral.
b: Primary viral pneumonia – progressive infiltrates, hypoxia, respiratory rate > 30/min; start supplemental oxygen, consider ICU transfer.
Bacterial superinfection – new fever after 5 days, lobar consolidation, purulent sputum; add appropriate antibiotics.
Severe dehydration – dry mucous membranes, oliguria; give IV crystalloids, monitor electrolytes.
Acute kidney injury – rising creatinine, oliguria; adjust drug dosing, consider renal replacement if severe.
Myocarditis or pericarditis – chest pain, tachycardia, ECG changes; obtain cardiac enzymes, refer to cardiology.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities modify presentation, diagnostic accuracy, and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV – lower CD4 may blunt fever, increase viral shedding; start oseltamivir regardless of CD4, monitor for opportunistic infections.
TB – chronic cough may mask influenza; obtain sputum GeneXpert if TB suspected, continue anti‑TB drugs.
Malnutrition – impaired immunity, higher risk of severe disease; give high‑calorie feeds, monitor electrolytes.
Pregnancy – higher oxygen requirement, altered drug pharmacokinetics; maintain SpO₂ ≥95%, use oseltamivir (category C but safe).
Diabetes – hyperglycaemia worsens outcomes; check glucose, adjust insulin, avoid high‑dose steroids.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort) – induce CYP enzymes, reduce oseltamivir levels; advise discontinuation.
Alcohol abuse – worsens liver function, increases bleeding risk with NSAIDs; prefer paracetamol.
Renal failure – oseltamivir dose adjustment needed; use renal‑adjusted regimen, avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics.
Liver failure – limit paracetamol, monitor transaminases; consider alternative antipyretics.

sections.p: Tailored strategies address the unique needs of vulnerable populations in low‑resource environments.
b: Children – give oseltamivir for any severe case or for children <5 years with complicated illness; monitor for vomiting, give with food.
Pregnant women – maintain higher oxygen targets, use oseltamivir, avoid NSAIDs in third trimester, monitor fetal heart rate if possible.
Elderly – lower threshold for hospitalisation, watch for atypical presentations (confusion), start antivirals early, consider pneumococcal vaccine status.
People with HIV – treat as high‑risk, ensure drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals are checked (avoid protease inhibitors that inhibit CYP3A4).
Low‑resource settings – rely on clinical ILI definition, use rapid antigen test only if available, prioritize oral oseltamivir, use pulse oximetry for oxygen targets, arrange referral early.

sections.p: Sample questions to test mastery of influenza management in low‑resource contexts.

t.a: What three historical elements are essential when evaluating a patient with suspected influenza?
t.b: Onset time, vaccination status, and presence of high‑risk comorbidities.

t.a: Describe how to perform and interpret the auscultatory finding that suggests viral versus bacterial pneumonia.
t.b: Diffuse crackles without focal consolidation suggest viral; localized bronchial breath sounds with egophony suggest bacterial.

t.a: When rapid antigen testing is unavailable, what clinical criteria define influenza‑like illness?
t.b: Fever ≥ 38 °C plus cough or sore throat with symptom onset ≤ 7 days.

t.a: Which laboratory result would prompt addition of empiric antibiotics in a patient already on oseltamivir?
t.b: New leukocytosis > 12 × 10⁹/L with a left shift or a chest X‑ray showing lobar consolidation.

t.a: Explain why neuraminidase inhibition reduces viral spread.
t.b: It prevents cleavage of sialic acid, trapping virions on the host cell surface and limiting release of new particles.

t.a: A child with influenza deteriorates on day 5 with persistent fever. What is the next investigation?
t.b: Obtain a chest radiograph to look for secondary bacterial pneumonia; consider blood cultures if febrile.

t.a: List two adverse effects of oseltamivir and the immediate actions required.
t.b: Nausea – give with food; neuropsychiatric symptoms – monitor, consider switching to inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor.

t.a: When should a patient with influenza be referred to a higher‑level facility?
t.b: If SpO₂ < 90% despite oxygen, respiratory rate > 30/min, altered mental status, or multi‑organ dysfunction.

t.a: How does HIV infection modify the interpretation of a normal white‑cell count in influenza?
t.b: HIV may blunt leukocytosis; a normal count does not exclude severe infection, so rely on clinical severity.

facts: Influenza incubation period: 1‑4 days, median 2 days.
Peak viral shedding: 24‑48 h after symptom onset, continues up to 7 days in adults, 10 days in children.
High‑risk groups: pregnant women, children <5 yr, elderly ≥65 yr, HIV, chronic heart/lung disease.
Oxygen target: SpO₂ ≥93 % (≥95 % in pregnant women).
Oseltamivir should be started ≤48 h from symptom onset for severe or high‑risk cases.
Neuraminidase inhibitor effect: blocks release of progeny virions from infected cells.
Antigenic shift occurs when reassortment between human and animal influenza A strains creates a novel HA/NA combination.
Rapid influenza diagnostic test (RIDT) sensitivity 50‑70 %, specificity >90 %; confirm with RT‑PCR if available.
Bacterial superinfection most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae.
Seasonal peaks in East Africa usually coincide with the long rainy season (April‑June).

vivas.q: Define antigenic shift and give an example of when it occurs in influenza.
vivas.a: Antigenic shift is the abrupt emergence of a new HA and/or NA subtype due to reassortment of gene segments between human and animal influenza A viruses, e.g., H1N1 2009 pandemic.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line antiviral for severe influenza and how does it work?
vivas.a: Oseltamivir, a neuraminidase inhibitor; it blocks neuraminidase, preventing cleavage of sialic acid and thus release of new virions.

vivas.q: A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman presents with fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain. What is the next best step?
vivas.a: Obtain a chest X‑ray to look for influenza‑associated viral pneumonia or bacterial superinfection; start oseltamivir promptly.

vivas.q: Explain why NSAIDs are avoided in severe influenza.
vivas.a: NSAIDs can mask fever, increase risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, and may worsen renal function in dehydrated patients.

vivas.q: A patient on oseltamivir develops nausea. How should you manage it?
vivas.a: Continue therapy; advise taking with food or a small snack to reduce gastrointestinal upset.

vivas.q: How does rapid influenza diagnostic test (RIDT) differ from RT‑PCR in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: RIDT gives results in 15‑30 min, is cheap but less sensitive; RT‑PCR is more sensitive and specific but requires laboratory capacity.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions for suspected influenza?
vivas.a: Onset and duration of fever, cough, myalgia; exposure to sick contacts; vaccination status; risk factors (pregnancy, HIV, chronic disease).

vivas.q: Describe the bedside examination for influenza‑associated pneumonia.
vivas.a: Inspect for respiratory distress; auscultate for crackles or bronchial breath sounds; assess oxygen saturation; note any pleural rubs indicating secondary bacterial infection.

vivas.q: Why is bacterial superinfection more common after influenza?
vivas.a: Influenza damages respiratory epithelium and impairs innate immunity, allowing colonising bacteria to invade lung tissue.

vivas.q: What is the primary function of the haemagglutinin (HA) protein?
vivas.a: Mediates viral attachment to host sialic acid receptors and fusion of viral and endosomal membranes.

vivas.q: A child with influenza has persistent fever after 5 days. What investigation is appropriate?
vivas.a: Obtain a chest X‑ray to rule out bacterial pneumonia; consider full blood count and blood cultures if febrile.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a negative RIDT in a high‑risk patient.
vivas.a: A negative result does not exclude influenza; proceed with empirical antiviral therapy if clinical suspicion is high.

vivas.q: What is the recommended management for an elderly patient with SpO₂ 88 % on room air?
vivas.a: Start supplemental oxygen to achieve SpO₂ ≥93 %; give oseltamivir; monitor for respiratory failure.

vivas.q: What is the consequence of neuraminidase inhibition on the viral life cycle?
vivas.a: Prevents release of newly formed virions, limiting spread to adjacent cells.

vivas.q: Which virological phenomenon describes the emergence of a novel influenza strain through major genomic segment exchange?
During viral entry, which influenza surface proteins mediate attachment to host cells?
vivas.a: Haemagglutinin (HA) binds sialic acid receptors; neuraminidase (NA) assists release later.

vivas.q: When is antigenic shift most likely to occur?
vivas.a: When a human influenza A virus co‑infects a cell with an avian or swine influenza A virus, allowing reassortment.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old man presents with sudden fever, myalgia and dry cough 24 h after symptom onset. He is immunocompromised. Which is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
o: Oseltamivir oral therapy
High‑dose paracetamol only
Empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics
Inhaled bronchodilators
mcqs.e: Oseltamivir should be started promptly in high‑risk patients within 48 h.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best describes antigenic shift in influenza viruses?
o: Minor point mutations in HA gene
Gradual loss of vaccine effectiveness
Reassortment of whole genome segments producing a novel HA/NA
Seasonal variation in virus circulation
mcqs.e: Shift is due to reassortment creating a new HA/NA combination.

mcqs.q: A rapid influenza test is negative in a child with classic symptoms during an outbreak. What is the next step?
o: Discharge without treatment
Order chest X‑ray
Start oseltamivir if high‑risk
Give amoxicillin
mcqs.e: A negative RIDT does not rule out influenza; treat high‑risk patients.

mcqs.q: Which surface protein of influenza virus is responsible for binding to host sialic acid receptors?
o: Neuraminidase
Matrix protein M2
Nucleoprotein
Haemagglutinin
mcqs.e: HA mediates attachment to sialic acid residues.

mcqs.q: In a pregnant woman with confirmed influenza, the recommended oxygen saturation target is:
Which complication is most commonly associated with influenza in low‑resource settings?
o: Myocarditis
Secondary bacterial pneumonia
Acute kidney injury
Pulmonary embolism
mcqs.e: Bacterial superinfection, especially pneumococcal pneumonia, is the commonest severe complication.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old patient with influenza has SpO₂ 88 % on room air. Which action is first?
o: Start high‑flow nasal cannula
Give oral oseltamivir only
Intubate immediately
Begin supplemental oxygen to reach ≥93 %
mcqs.e: First give supplemental oxygen to achieve target saturation.

mcqs.q: Which drug class should be avoided in severe influenza due to increased bleeding risk?
o: NSAIDs
Beta‑blockers
Corticosteroids
Macrolides
mcqs.e: NSAIDs can increase bleeding risk and mask fever.

cases.v: A 6‑year‑old boy presents with 3 days of fever 39 °C, sore throat, dry cough and myalgia. He is not vaccinated. Examination shows tachypnea, crackles at bases, SpO₂ 94 % on room air.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate antiviral indication?
qs.a: Start oseltamivir because he is a child with influenza symptoms and is at risk of complications.

qs.q: What bedside test helps differentiate viral from bacterial pneumonia?
qs.a: Absence of focal consolidation and normal white‑cell count favors viral; however, chest X‑ray is needed for definitive assessment.

qs.q: If the child deteriorates with SpO₂ falling to 90 %, what is the next step?
qs.a: Provide supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO₂ ≥93 % and reassess; consider hospital admission and possible antibiotics for superinfection.

cases.v: A 32‑year‑old pregnant woman (28 weeks) presents with sudden fever 38.5 °C, severe myalgia, dry cough and conjunctivitis. She reports no prior influenza vaccination.

qs.q: Which antiviral is recommended and is it safe in pregnancy?
qs.a: Oseltamivir is recommended; it is considered safe in pregnancy and benefits outweigh potential risks.

qs.q: What complication should be monitored for in late pregnancy?
qs.a: Watch for rapid progression to viral pneumonia and fetal distress; arrange obstetric review if respiratory failure develops.

mistakes: Targeting SpO₂ ≥93 % for pregnant women – the correct target is ≥95 % (or ≥94 %).
Stating neuraminidase prevents virion release – it actually facilitates release; inhibition blocks this step.
Omitting antiviral recommendation for children with severe or progressive disease.
Confusing antigenic drift with shift – shift involves reassortment of whole genome segments.
Assuming a negative rapid test rules out influenza in high‑risk patients.
Prescribing NSAIDs for severe influenza without noting bleeding and renal risks.
Failing to give supplemental oxygen before other interventions in hypoxic patients.
Not recognizing that bacterial superinfection can present with new focal crackles after initial viral phase.

What is the primary function of the haemagglutinin (HA) protein? — Mediates viral attachment to host sialic acid receptors and fusion of viral and endosomal membranes.

A child with influenza has persistent fever after 5 days. What investigation is appropriate? — Obtain a chest X‑ray to rule out bacterial pneumonia; consider full blood count and blood cultures if febrile.
Explain the significance of a negative RIDT in a high‑risk patient. — A negative result does not exclude influenza; proceed with empirical antiviral therapy if clinical suspicion is high.
What is the recommended management for an elderly patient with SpO₂ 88 % on room air? — Start supplemental oxygen to achieve SpO₂ ≥93 %; give oseltamivir; monitor for respiratory failure.
What is the consequence of neuraminidase inhibition on the viral life cycle? — Prevents release of newly formed virions, limiting spread to adjacent cells.
